gate:
Heat lives in some bodies that wants to be put to work. It is not ambition and it is not stamina, though it gets called both. It is closer to a generator built into the flesh, a current that produces more than the person carrying it needs, and feels best when the surplus is moving outward into the world as something other people can use. The current pulses. It surges, then rests, then surges again, and the rest is built in. It is not a failure of will.

What this drive wants is skillful power. Raw force bored a long time ago. The pull now is toward capacity, the kind of work that turns labor into resource, that feeds a household, a village, a life. A person carrying this often reads to others as a workhorse, or as someone who cannot sit still. The truer picture is finer. They are wired to make, and to make well, and the making is how the body knows it is alive. Pushed without rhythm, the engine cooks itself.
centre_field:
Inside the body is a motor that everything else borrows from when something actually has to get done. It is the part of you that knows yes by lighting up and knows no by going quiet. This drive is wired straight into it, with one specific job. The power here is not theoretical and it is not a decision made from the head. It is response. The motor turns on for the right work and refuses the wrong work, and the refusal is not stubbornness. It is the body protecting the engine from being run on the wrong fuel.

Honor the lighting up and the rhythm sustains itself across decades. Override it, push past the quiet no because someone needed something or the calendar said yes, and the same current that should generate resource turns acidic. Burnout, resentment, the slow corrosion of a life spent producing for purposes the body never agreed to. The yes is the whole instruction.
channel:
All this surplus, and on its own nowhere certain to take it. Energy without a heading builds the wrong things, fills rooms nobody asked for, generates resource that lands in the wrong hands. This code reaches for the other half of itself, the part that holds the slow inward compass, the quiet sense of which way a life is meant to face. The lineage calls this connection the rhythm of resource. The name fits.

When the compass meets the motor, the work lands where it was supposed to land. The day acquires a beat. Labor stops being exertion and becomes a kind of music, surplus pouring in the direction the self was already pointing toward before the head got involved. Without the compass, the power scatters and the person carrying it ends up exhausted by their own productivity. Joined, the two become something rarer, a life that produces real wealth and aims it at what was always meant to receive it.
